c.v: Answer in five or six sentences, without looking anything up. What are wall time, steady time and simulation time, and what can each of them do that the others can't? Which of them does a node's

Wall time, which ROS calls system time, is the computer's calendar clock, counted in nanoseconds since 1 January 1970. Two machines synchronised with NTP agree on it, which is why message stamps use it, but it jumps when NTP or an administrator corrects it. Steady time counts from an arbitrary start, on Linux the boot, and only ever moves forward at a constant rate. It is the clock for measuring durations and hardware timeouts, and its value means nothing on another machine. Simulation time is the simulator's clock: Gazebo publishes it on
, it stops while the simulation is paused, and it runs faster or slower than wall time when the real-time factor isn't 1. A node's

A node has three clocks. System time, ROS's wall time, is the computer's calendar clock, counted from 1970; two machines synchronised with NTP agree on it, but it jumps when that correction runs. Steady time counts from an arbitrary start, only moving forward at a constant rate, meaning nothing on another machine but never jumping. ROS time is what a node's
returns: system time by default, or, when
is true, the latest value published on

The problem is that a message stamped by one node must mean the same thing to another, and a duration measured on one machine must never jump backward mid-measurement, and no single clock does both. Message headers need a clock two machines agree on, ruling out steady time; a duration or a hardware timeout needs a clock that never jumps, ruling out system time when corrected. A simulated robot also needs a clock every node agrees on that can pause and run at other than real speed, which neither other can do.
ROS time makes this possible: with
false it is system time; with it true the node subscribes to
and reports the latest value, standing still while paused and running at whatever rate the simulator publishes.
runs on this clock, firing by simulated time and stopping with the simulation;

always runs on the steady clock regardless. A time value carries its clock type with it, so comparing two of different clocks fails outright rather than silently, which is how a mixed time base gets caught.
The mistake under pressure is a node reading a clock the rest of the system doesn't. One node left without

in a simulated system stamps messages in system time while every other node uses simulation time, so a consumer computes an age of decades. Simulation time can also jump backward, on a world reset or a looped replay, and any state remembering a past timestamp, a watchdog's last message time, a rate estimate, has no reason to notice: it keeps comparing against a stamp time has passed twice, calling stale data fresh until real time catches up.
